conflicts.fact: Whether the generator magnet(s) are stationary or rotating, and what the 'housing' is, in the Kericho generator
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1: the coils rotate near magnets. Lesson 3: the coils rotate inside a housing that functions like a giant U-shaped magnet. Lesson 4: coils rotate relative to fixed magnets (or electromagnets). Lesson 6: coils are wound around strong electromagnet cores, so the coil and core are conflated. Mostly consistent, but Lesson 7 calls the iron core a 'stator' while the coils rotate.

conflicts.fact: Wire length and number of turns in electromagnet/bell builds, and the dry-cell wiring
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1: 30 cm of wire, 15 turns around the nail. Lesson 7: about 1 m of wire, at least 30 turns. Different activities, so only a minor inconsistency.

conflicts.fact: The generator magnet type and strength claim for soft iron cores vs steel
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 says soft iron is used in generator cores because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised, whereas Lesson 2 says engineers protect generator magnets from heat and shock because domain disorder means power failure. Lessons 2 and 3 treat the generator's magnets as permanent magnets, in contrast to Lesson 1's soft iron temporary cores.

conflicts.fact: Which magnetisation method gives the strongest magnet / the induction method's permanence
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 says stroking gave the strongest magnet on average, while the Learned section says the induction method produces the weakest permanent magnet. Soft iron is only temporarily magnetised by induction and by electrical means, so calling the induction result a permanent magnet conflicts with the definition of the electrical method as temporary.

conflicts.fact: Why stopping the generator/dynamo stops current
conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 says stopping the wheel is functionally equivalent to demagnetisation and domain disorder (the ordered relationship collapses, and heat or vibration means power failure). Lessons 4, 5 and 8 say that with no relative motion there is no flux change, so no e.m.f. is induced, and the magnet stays magnetised. These are incompatible explanations.
Lesson 1 gives the Form One student from Kericho no name, Lessons 4 and 5 call her Akoth, and Lesson 7 refers only to 'the Kericho student'. Minor, but the naming is inconsistent.

conflicts.fact: The bell's make-and-break cycle is the same as polarity switching and induced e.m.f. factors
conflicts.versions: Lesson 7 says the bell's magnetisation/demagnetisation cycle is the same principle as switching polarity in a generator's rotating coil, and says coil turns and current strength are factors affecting induced e.m.f. Lesson 5 says induced e.m.f. depends on the speed, magnet strength, turns and angle of relative motion, with no role for current strength. The bell has no induction.

Lesson 4 uses a straight conductor moved between the poles of a U-shaped magnet. Lesson 5 uses a bar magnet pushed into a coil. Lesson 5 also states the angle of entry gives zero e.m.f. at 0°, consistent with Lesson 4's parallel result, but the angle at which the intermediate deflection occurs differs in framing (45° vs 90°/0° only).

conflicts.fact: Number of factors affecting induced e.m.f.
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 and Lesson 8 list four factors (speed, field strength, turns, angle). Lesson 6 lists only three: speed of rotation, number of coil turns and strength of the magnetic field.

Lesson 6 says step-up transformers at Olkaria raise voltage to 132 kV, but Lesson 5 says Tana River hydroelectric and Olkaria generators 'produce thousands of volts' directly. Lesson 6's Kericho dormitory 240 V is the same figure used elsewhere, so no conflict there.
